title: Sustainable Shipping Initiative and partners target ‘blue shipping corridors’ to harmonise shipping decarbonisation with better ocean health
summary: The Sustainable Shipping Initiative (SSI) and over 35 partners are now pushing for 'blue shipping corridors,' a conceptual expansion of 'green corridors' to integrate 'ocean health' with decarbonisation talks. This COP31 'Ambition Statement' outlines a vision for zero-emission routes and marine conservation, yet primarily focuses on 'enabling environments' and annual progress reviews, rather than concrete regulation. While the rhetoric includes 'nature-positive port design' and 'smarter routing,' it offers little immediate impact on the carbon intensity of today's global fleet or the persistent usage of heavy fuel oil.
content:
The Sustainable Shipping Initiative (SSI) has called on governments to help establish ‘blue shipping corridors’, extending the role of green corridors, established to accelerate decarbonisation in key shipping lanes, to include ocean health. SSI is co-leading the statement through the Marine Biodiversity and Ocean Health Breakthrough, the initiative that started this process, and identified that decarbonisation and ocean health are two sides of the same coin.

The statement, COP31 Blue Shipping Corridors Ambition Statement, is backed by more than 35 organisations from across shipping, ports, finance, science and conservation, including WWF, World Resources Institute, the UN Global Compact, Ocean Conservancy, IFAW, Lloyd’s Register Foundation, Transport & Environment, Jotun, Plymouth Marine Laboratory and GRID-Arendal. Together they are making the case that green corridors for ships, which are dedicated maritime trade routes where zero-emission and low-carbon shipping is developed, can do the same for ocean conservation, marine life and coastal communities. Green corridors have become one of shipping’s most practical tools for convening first movers, fuel suppliers, ports and cargo owners around shared decarbonisation decisions on a defined route.

The new Ambition Statement, drafted by the Marrakech Partnership Maritime Stakeholders, sets out a vision for corridors that enable zero- or near-zero-emission shipping, deliver significant ocean conservation measures at sea and in port with a net positive impact on ocean health and marine biodiversity, and bring real benefits to coastal communities without harming biodiversity on land. Endorsers commit to working towards an enabling environment that covers everything from nature-positive port design and smarter routing to better ocean data, a skilled workforce, a just transition for remote and underserved ports, and an annual review of progress.

Many of the solutions dovetail, offering dual benefits to the climate and the oceans. For example, International Maritime Organisation (IMO) research found that a layer of slime as thin as 0.5mm covering up to half a hull can push GHG emissions up by 20–25%, while the same fouling carries invasive species into new seas. A clean hull cuts fuel bills, emissions and the spread of invaders in one go. In the same way, slowing ships in hotspots not only reduces underwater noise, emissions and air pollution for coastal communities, it also prevents collisions with whales.

Today’s announcement builds upon SSI’s Shipping and Ocean Health 2026 Report which shows that the actions that decarbonise shipping can often protect the seas at little or no additional cost. However, progress has been held back by access to finance, cross-sector collaboration and a clear business case, all of which blue corridors are well placed to help overcome.

Ellie Besley-Gould, Chief Executive Officer, Sustainable Shipping Initiative, said: “Green corridors have shown what’s possible when shipowners, ports, fuel suppliers and governments commit to a route together. Blue shipping corridors take that model and recognise that if we’re already rethinking these routes from the ground up, it makes complete sense to make them better for the ocean at the same time. So many of the measures that cut emissions, like cleaner hulls and slower, smarter voyages, also take pressure off marine life, often at little or no extra cost. It would be a real missed opportunity not to capture those wins. The industry is ready to step up and earnestly support action in this space. What we need now is for governments to put the conditions in place so it can.”
